arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Theodore Olson argued Congress created a specific enforcement scheme for ERISA violations.
Olson stated the opposing sides seek equitable remedies for misleading summaries, not direct benefit recovery.
Kneedler argued pension benefits are a major component of employee compensation.
Bruce argued detrimental reliance is not found in the ERISA summary requirement section.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests whether a summary document can override the formal pension plan. Employees rely on the summary to claim lost money. Cigna insists the formal plan controls all benefits.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on November 30, 2010.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Employees want a court order requiring Cigna to pay the pension benefits they lost due to the misleading summary.
Cigna wants the court to reject the claim that the summary changed the plan and deny the lost benefit payments.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Employees argue the summary created a binding promise that Cigna must honor to prevent unfair loss of compensation.
Cigna argues the summary is merely informational and cannot legally amend the formal plan document that governs benefits.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Scalia asked whether items in the summary must exist in the formal plan to be valid.
Justice Ginsburg asked if the lower court treated the summary as an amendment or just a description of the plan.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This dispute determines whether employees can recover lost pension money based on a summary document. It defines the legal weight of plan summaries versus formal plan documents. It affects how companies communicate benefit changes to workers.
